findings.claim: “Three ethical issues are required at GCSE: informed consent, confidentiality and harm to participants.” Repeated in a Key Fact, in its data-revision-tip and in the conclusion.
findings.truth: The ethics section of the spec requires four: informed consent, confidentiality, harm to participants and deception (plus the strategies sociologists use to address them). Telling students only three are required invites them to skip deception, which the lesson itself then teaches in the collapsible, the glossary and the knowledge-check matcher.
findings.evidence: spec section 4.5 Ethical issues affecting research

findings.claim: “feminists argue falling rates in recent decades may reflect legal reforms giving women greater economic independence.”
findings.truth: Reversed. Feminists explain the long RISE in divorce after 1969 by legal reform and women's growing economic independence, which made it possible to leave an unhappy marriage. The fall since the 1990s peak is normally explained by fewer marriages and more cohabitation, not by women's independence. A student reproducing the sentence would attribute the wrong argument to feminism.
findings.evidence: standard GCSE sociology of the family; Divorce Reform Act 1969 (in force 1971); ONS divorce numbers peak 1993

findings.claim: Model answer to the 9-mark question: “the Crime Survey for England and Wales provides data on millions of households.”
findings.truth: The CSEW interviews about 31,000 adults aged 16+ a year, plus about 1,500 children aged 10-15. It is a sample survey of tens of thousands, not millions. Its real strength is that it counts crimes never reported to the police.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Crime Survey for England and Wales (ONS figures)

findings.claim: “The examiner is looking for you to compare at least two named perspectives and reach a supported judgement.”
findings.truth: The spec sets no such rule. AO3 asks students to analyse and evaluate in order to construct arguments, make judgements and draw conclusions; the number of perspectives is not prescribed anywhere in the spec, and no mark scheme is quoted. Stated in the examiner's voice it reads as an invented mark-scheme requirement.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1 assessment objectives; spec prints no question ladder

findings.claim: “The mark scheme rewards practical reasoning in context.”
findings.truth: An assertion about unseen mark-scheme content. The teaching point is sound; the mark-scheme voice is not. The house rule keeps board mark-scheme wording and claims out of student-facing text.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md copyright-distancing rule; spec prints no mark schemes

findings.claim: “The mark scheme rewards candidates who use the data throughout their argument, not those who mention it once and then ignore it.”
findings.truth: Same pattern as F5: an assertion about unseen mark-scheme content. The advice survives as a plain instruction to the student.

findings.claim: The whole lesson - research design (aim, hypothesis, operationalisation, method choice, pilot study, sampling, analysis, mixed methods) and interpreting graphs, charts and tables - sits in a unit built on the first component's research-methods topic.
findings.truth: That material is spec sections 7.1 and 7.2, Applied methods of sociological enquiry, which belongs to the SECOND component. The first component's methods topic is 4.1-4.5 (types of data, methods, sampling, practical issues, ethical issues) and does not include research design or data interpretation. Nothing here misleads a student about the exam - both components are compulsory, the lesson claims no paper, and the spec says methods permeate the course - so the question is placement, not correctness. Options: (a) leave it here and make sure the second component's applied-methods unit does not repeat it; (b) move it there and shorten this unit to five lessons.
findings.ruling: NOTE: L6 applied-methods content belongs to Component 2 by spec numbering, but no paper is named and both components are compulsory; left. Crime-deviance unit's applied lessons (L7-L8) cover the same ground - overlap recorded.

findings.claim: The unit teaches a fixed question ladder across all six lessons: 1-mark multiple choice, 2-mark Define, 3-mark Identify and Describe, 4-mark Describe, 9-mark Discuss, 12-mark Evaluate.
findings.truth: The spec prints no question ladder, so the tariffs cannot be verified from it. Nothing in the ladder contradicts the confirmed facts (each written exam 1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks, 50% of the qualification; at least 15% of marks on research methods; AO1 40 / AO2 40 / AO3 20), and no impossible tariff, SPaG claim or other board's paper name appears anywhere in the unit. Recorded, not edited.

findings.claim: “Becker's concept of master status” (also the fourth knowledge check and a flashcard).
findings.truth: Master status was coined by Everett Hughes in 1945; Becker adopted it in Outsiders (1963), which the lesson dates correctly. The attribution is standard GCSE textbook usage and the spec names Becker for labelling, so it is left as it stands.
findings.evidence: spec 6.4 (Becker, labelling and the deviant career); Hughes 1945

findings.claim: “the New Right perspective appears throughout the GCSE Sociology specification, particularly in relation to the family, poverty and crime.”
findings.truth: The spec names the New Right for the family (2.4) and Murray's underclass under poverty (5.5). The crime section lists functionalist, subcultural, Marxist, interactionist and feminist explanations only. Murray's thesis does bear on crime patterns, so the sentence is defensible; left as it stands.

findings.claim: Two further examiner-voice lines: “immediately signals to the examiner that you are operating at the level of sociological analysis” (lesson 2) and “The examiner is looking for a reasoned judgement, not a balanced description” (lesson 3).
findings.truth: Both restate AO3 fairly rather than inventing a rule, so they are left as they stand. F4, F5 and F6 are fixed because each asserts a specific requirement or reward that the spec never states.

summary: Six lessons checked against the spec. Two HIGH factual errors: a reversed feminist argument about divorce rates (lesson 6) and an invented CSEW sample size in a mark scheme (lesson 4). One scope error: the ethics section teaches three required ethical issues where the spec requires four, omitting deception (lesson 5). Three fabricated examiner or mark-scheme claims removed. Sociologist attributions, dates and studies otherwise check out (Genie 1970 California age 13; Willis 1977, twelve lads; Becker Outsiders 1963; Walby's six structures; Parsons on primary socialisation; Oakley on gender socialisation; Durkheim, Davis and Moore, Bowles and Gintis, Halsey, Murray). Reliability and validity are defined the right way round. All 30 knowledge-check answer keys were recomputed and are correct. No board name appears anywhere in student-facing prose, and no banned string is present.
